<meta>continues from previous page: ...as if the spirits were present. To avoid deceiving them is also a way of instruction. He asked about everything from the dance of the eight rows to the sacrifice at Mount Tai. Because the [rites] were lost, the Master's grief and sorrow were entirely in agreement with the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals. Master Zhu said: "This is..."</meta>

○ The Master said, "The gentleman <term>junzi</term> <gloss>noble person/gentleman</gloss> has nothing to contend for. If he must, perhaps it is in archery. With bows and yielding, they ascend; upon descending, they drink. Their contention is that of a gentleman." <note>The character for 'contention' <term>zheng</term> is pronounced in the departing tone.</note>

"With bows and yielding, they ascend" refers to the ritual of the great archery ceremony. One bows three times before ascending the hall. <note>Mr. Hu says:</note> In the ritual of archery, the archery official <term>si-she</term> <gloss>official in charge of archery rites</gloss> calls out three pairs of archers. The three pairs emerge from their tents, face west, and bow. When they arrive below the steps, they face north and bow; when they reach the steps, they bow. This is what is meant by "three bows before ascending the hall."

"Upon descending, they drink" refers to the fact that after the archery is completed, they bow and descend to wait for all the pairs to descend. The winners then bow, and the losers ascend to retrieve the <margin>Explanation of sounds</margin>
arrows and place them. They stand to drink. <note>Mr. Hu says: When the archery is finished, they face north and bow, just as they did when ascending. When the archery is over, they return to their tents.</note>

When the pairs have finished their archery, they also do this. This is what is meant by "after the archery is completed, they bow and descend to..."

<summary>This passage examines the Confucian concept of noble competition through the lens of the traditional archery ritual, emphasizing that the gentleman's conduct is defined by courtesy and humility rather than personal victory.</summary>
<keywords>Confucius, Archery Ritual, Junzi, Ritual Propriety, Master Zhu, Hu Family</keywords>
